reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Middleton's Allergy
clinicalPearls: True drug allergy is an immune-mediated subset of adverse drug reactions and must be distinguished from predictable dose-related side effects and non-immune intolerance

The Gell and Coombs framework is useful: immediate IgE-mediated reactions (type I) cause urticaria, angioedema, and anaphylaxis, while delayed T-cell-mediated reactions (type IV) cause most drug-induced rashes
The tempo matters: immediate reactions arise within minutes to an hour of exposure, whereas delayed maculopapular eruptions and severe cutaneous reactions typically appear days into a course

Beta-lactam antibiotics are the commonest cause of drug-induced anaphylaxis, but a reported penicillin allergy is frequently inaccurate and unnecessarily drives use of broader, more toxic alternatives

Severe cutaneous adverse reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and DRESS are potentially fatal and are suggested by mucosal involvement, skin pain, blistering, fever, facial oedema, and organ dysfunction
Skin testing is validated mainly for penicillins and perioperative agents; specific IgE and in-vitro tests are limited, so the supervised graded challenge remains the definitive test for many drugs
Management principles are immediate cessation of the culprit drug, treatment of the reaction, clear documentation and patient warning, and selection of a structurally unrelated alternative
Desensitisation can allow temporary tolerance when a culprit drug is essential and no alternative exists, but it is contraindicated in severe cutaneous reactions such as SJS/TEN and DRESS
Careful de-labelling of unverified penicillin allergy through history and, where appropriate, challenge is an important antimicrobial-stewardship intervention
reference.pathophysiology: Immune-mediated drug reactions occur when a drug or its reactive metabolite, often after binding host protein as a hapten, is recognised by the adaptive immune system. Type I reactions involve drug-specific IgE on mast cells and basophils, producing immediate mediator release. Type II reactions are antibody-mediated cytotoxicity against drug-coated cells (e.g. immune haemolysis, thrombocytopenia), and type III reactions involve immune-complex deposition (serum sickness, vasculitis). Type IV delayed reactions are T-cell-driven and range from benign exanthems to severe cutaneous reactions; the p-i concept describes direct, non-covalent drug interaction with immune receptors, and specific HLA alleles predispose to particular severe reactions.
additionalDifferentials: Viral exanthem coinciding with drug therapy
Direct mast-cell activation (e.g. by opioids, vancomycin infusion reaction)
NSAID- or ACE-inhibitor-induced angioedema through non-IgE mechanisms
Underlying autoimmune or infectious disease producing rash or organ dysfunction
Chronic spontaneous urticaria unrelated to the drug
additionalInvestigations: Skin prick and intradermal testing where validated (penicillins, perioperative agents)
Serum drug-specific IgE where available and serum tryptase during acute reactions
Supervised graded drug challenge to confirm or exclude allergy
Delayed-reading intradermal or patch testing for suspected type IV reactions
HLA genotyping before selected high-risk drugs where guidelines recommend it
Blood count, eosinophils, liver and renal function in suspected DRESS or systemic involvement
redFlags: Anaphylaxis with hypotension or airway compromise requiring immediate intramuscular adrenaline
Mucosal erosions, skin blistering or pain, or positive Nikolsky sign suggesting SJS/TEN
Fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and organ involvement suggesting DRESS
Any severe cutaneous adverse reaction, in which re-exposure or desensitisation is contraindicated
reference.prognosis: Most benign exanthems and immediate reactions resolve fully once the drug is withdrawn and future exposure avoided. Severe cutaneous adverse reactions carry significant morbidity and mortality, particularly toxic epidermal necrolysis, and require urgent specialist and supportive care.
pitfalls: Accepting an unverified allergy label and defaulting to broader, more toxic alternatives
Attempting desensitisation or re-challenge after a severe cutaneous reaction
Mistaking a viral rash or predictable side effect for true allergy, or vice versa
Failing to document the reaction clearly and counsel the patient about cross-reacting agents
management: Immediately withdraw and clearly document the suspected culprit drug, and counsel the patient to avoid it and cross-reacting agents in future
Treat anaphylaxis with intramuscular adrenaline as first-line, together with oxygen, fluid resuscitation and airway support, using antihistamines and corticosteroids only as adjuncts

Recognise severe cutaneous adverse reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS) as emergencies requiring urgent drug cessation and supportive care in a specialist or burns unit, with systemic immunomodulation as indicated
Manage milder immediate or delayed reactions symptomatically with antihistamines and topical or oral corticosteroids

Confirm or refute the diagnosis with allergy testing, using skin prick and intradermal testing for penicillins and perioperative agents and a supervised graded challenge, to enable de-labelling of inaccurate penicillin-allergy records
Consider supervised drug desensitisation where an implicated drug is essential and irreplaceable
Refer to allergy and immunology, provide written allergy documentation and a patient alert, and check HLA genotyping before selected high-risk drugs where guidelines advise
